metadata.note: The Cotton Belt — the St. Louis Southwestern Railway — which is the answer to 'did the Southern Pacific have passenger rail from St. Louis to Texas?'. It did, but not over its own rails and not under its own name: SP bought about 87% of the Cotton Belt's stock on 14 April 1932 precisely to get an eastern gateway at St. Louis and Memphis, and the Cotton Belt went on running the trains under its own name and management until SP absorbed it in 1992. Three features, drawn 1882–1959: the St. Louis – Dallas main passenger route (746 mi as drawn), the main line's western end from the Dallas branch junction at Addison to Fort Worth, and the Texas main line from Mount Pleasant through Tyler and Corsicana to Waco. Added 2026-08-27.
metadata.how_st_louis_was_reached: The Cotton Belt's own rails ended at Illmo, Missouri. From 15 October 1900 it ran into St. Louis Union Station on trackage rights over the St. Louis, Iron Mountain and Southern (Missouri Pacific) — 123.7 miles to Valley Junction, Illinois, on the Illinois-side line through Gorham and Chester, crossing the Mississippi on the jointly-owned Thebes Bridge from 1905. The first 130 miles of the St. Louis – Dallas feature are therefore drawn on Missouri Pacific track. It carries the Cotton Belt's colour because the Cotton Belt ran the trains, per CLAUDE.md Rule 4.
metadata.why_not_southern_pacific_colour: Every feature here is coloured as the Cotton Belt and not as Southern Pacific, including the segments after April 1932. SP's holding was stock control, not a lease or a merger: the operating company on the timetable, the equipment and the depots stayed the St. Louis Southwestern Railway until 1992, decades after the last passenger train. Rule 4's split-at-the-change-of-operator test therefore does not fire here — the operator never changed during the drawn era. The SP relationship is instead named in every post-1932 segment note.
metadata.trains_drawn: Lone Star Limited (from 1928), Morning Star (1941–1952, St. Louis – Dallas overnight with a Memphis section connecting to Southern Railway's Tennessean), and unnamed trains 7 and 8 (1952–1959). The Memphis – Dallas Lone Star, which ran via Brinkley and Shreveport, is NOT drawn — the question this layer answers was about St. Louis.
metadata.not_drawn: The Tyler – Lufkin doodlebug, the Waco – Gatesville tail beyond Waco, the Commerce – Sherman and Corsicana – Hillsboro branches, and the Memphis and Shreveport lines. All carried passengers at some point and all are candidates for a later pass; none is drawn because no dates were checked for them.
metadata.not_yet_sourced: (1) The month in 1959 when trains 7 and 8 stopped running through to Texas. Sources agree the last train, No. 8 on 30 November 1959, ran only Pine Bluff – East St. Louis, and that by mid-1959 that was the only service left; the St. Louis – Dallas feature is drawn to 1959 across its whole length, which over-states the Texas end by some months. (2) One source says the final Texas operation was an overnight St. Louis – Dallas train calling at Tyler, and another says trains 7 and 8 ran between Tyler and St. Louis; Tyler is not on the Commerce – Greenville – Addison line that the 1941 timetable's mileages describe, so the late-1950s routing may have been Mount Pleasant – Tyler instead. Unresolved: the drawn route follows the 1941 timetable. (3) Fort Worth branch completion is given as July 1887 in one place and as rails reaching Grapevine in 1888 in another; drawn from 1888. (4) The year Mount Pleasant – Tyler – Waco lost its last passenger train; 1958, the date of the Gatesville mixed train's discontinuance, is used as a stand-in. (5) Every headway_min in this layer is an estimate.

properties.speed_source: Computed from the June 1941 timetable of the Morning Star (train 5): St. Louis Union Station 11:15P to Dallas Union Depot 8:50P, 756.2 miles in 21h35m, which is 35 mph / 56 km/h including every intermediate stop. The two intermediate checks agree: St. Louis to Brinkley (343.7 mi) in 10h10m is 34 mph, Brinkley to Dallas (412.5 mi) in 11h00m is 37.5 mph. This is a whole-route average and says nothing about track speed.
properties.geometry_quality: Traced from OpenStreetMap in four pieces, with two labelled approximations at the Dallas end. (1) St. Louis Union Station – Valley Junction/Dupo – Chester – Gorham – Thebes, 130.4 mi, routed over ways carrying old_railway_operator=MP (UP's Chester Subdivision) — this is the Missouri Pacific / Iron Mountain trackage the Cotton Belt used under its 1900 rights agreement, not Cotton Belt rails; the June 1941 timetable makes it 138.2 mi to Illmo against 130.4 traced, the difference being the terminal approach and the Washington Ave. stop. (2) Illmo – Dexter – Paragould – Jonesboro – Brinkley – Stuttgart – Pine Bluff – Fordyce – Camden – Lewisville – Texarkana – Mount Pleasant, 484.4 mi, entirely on ways tagged old_railway_operator=SSW (UP's Jonesboro and Pine Bluff Subdivisions), with one 0.09 km connector; the timetable's Illmo–Brinkley 205.5 mi against 204.8 traced. (3) Mount Pleasant – Mount Vernon – Sulphur Springs – Commerce – Greenville – Wylie – Plano – Addison, 118.6 mi on SSW-tagged rail (Blacklands Railway, CPKC Alliance Subdivision, DGNO) plus ONE STRAIGHT-LINE LEG OF 8.0 mi (12.9 km) between 33.0365,-96.3744 near Nevada, TX and 33.0963,-96.2555 west of Greenville, where the abandoned alignment is not mapped in OSM at all. (4) The Addison–Dallas branch, 13.4 mi against a documented 12: 2.4 mi traced on razed and abandoned ways still named 'Saint Louis Southwestern Railway', then 9.3 mi APPROXIMATED on the centreline of the Dallas North Tollway, which was built on the branch's right of way after the 1965 abandonment, then 1.8 mi of STRAIGHT LINE into Union Station. There is also a 163 m joint gap at Illmo where the MoPac trace meets the Cotton Belt trace. Whole feature 746.4 mi drawn against 756.2 mi in the June 1941 timetable (98.7%). Douglas-Peucker simplified at 15 m. Straight-line repair 2026-08-29: 9 ruled segments totalling 147 mi replaced with OpenStreetMap-traced rail geometry (see geometry_repairs for the OSM lines each one followed).

segments.note: The Cotton Belt reached St. Louis on 15 October 1900, when it agreed trackage rights over the St. Louis, Iron Mountain and Southern (Missouri Pacific) from Illmo into St. Louis Union Station — 123.7 miles of somebody else's railroad to reach the Gateway City. The Thebes Bridge, a five-span cantilever built jointly with the MoPac, Frisco and C&EI, opened in 1905 and put the Illinois-side route through Gorham and Thebes into use; the drawn era starts there rather than in 1900 because the pre-1905 crossing was by ferry at Gray's Point and is not the alignment drawn here. Illmo became the division point where crews changed and the dispatcher took over everything south to Pine Bluff. The Lone Star Limited began in 1928. headway_min of 720 stands for roughly two trains each way per day in this era and is an ESTIMATE, not read off a timetable.
sources: NOT SOURCED AT SEGMENT LEVEL: the 1900 trackage-rights agreement, the 1905 bridge and the 1928 Lone Star Limited are each carried by the references below, but nobody has checked a timetable for the number of trains, and the 1905 start year is this map's own choice of when the drawn alignment came into use.

segments.note: Southern Pacific bought about 87% of the Cotton Belt's stock on 14 April 1932, specifically to reach St. Louis and Memphis, and this is the era in which a St. Louis – Texas passenger train was an SP-controlled operation — though the Cotton Belt kept its own name, management and timetables, and SP did not run these trains itself. The St. Louis – Dallas train became the Morning Star in 1941, with a Memphis section added the same year to connect with the Southern Railway's new Tennessean. June 1941: train 5 left St. Louis Union Station at 11:15P and reached Dallas Union Depot at 8:50P the next evening, 756.2 miles, with coaches, sleepers and a diner. Through connections onto parent SP carried passengers on to San Antonio, El Paso and Los Angeles. headway_min of 1440 is one train each way per day, matching the 1941 timetable's single overnight schedule.
sources: Segment-level: the 14 April 1932 SP purchase, the 1941 renaming and Memphis section, and the schedule and mileage are read from the references below; the 1941 timetable is reproduced at streamlinerschedules.com.

segments.note: The Cotton Belt was one of the first Class I railroads in the southwest to quit the passenger business. The Morning Star name went away in the November 1952 restructuring, replaced by unnamed trains 7 and 8 on the same St. Louis – Dallas overnight run — coaches and sleepers kept, food service cut. The Texas end was pared back during 1959, so that by mid-year the only Cotton Belt passenger service left was between East St. Louis and Pine Bluff; the last train, No. 8, ran from Pine Bluff to East St. Louis on 30 November 1959. headway_min of 1440 is one train each way per day.
sources: Segment-level: the November 1952 restructuring, trains 7 and 8, and the 30 November 1959 last run are carried by the references below. The month in 1959 when the Dallas end stopped is NOT SOURCED — see the layer's not_yet_sourced note.

properties.speed_source: ESTIMATE, not sourced. No timetable for the Fort Worth end was found; 45 km/h (28 mph) is a guess at a branch local making every stop between Addison and Fort Worth.
properties.geometry_quality: Traced from OpenStreetMap end to end with no approximated leg and no connectors: 38.2 mi over ways tagged old_railway_operator=SSW, which today carry TEXRail west of Grapevine and the CPKC Alliance Subdivision east of it. The one thing to distrust is the last mile into Fort Worth, drawn on TEXRail's present-day approach to Fort Worth Central Station rather than on the 1900–2002 Union Depot's own throat. Douglas-Peucker simplified at 15 m.

segments.note: The Cotton Belt's own main line west of the Dallas branch junction at Addison, through Carrollton and Grapevine into Fort Worth. The St. Louis, Arkansas and Texas completed the Mount Pleasant – Fort Worth line in July 1887 and the rails reached Grapevine in 1888; Grapevine's depot dates from about 1901. Fort Worth, not Dallas, was the Cotton Belt's western terminus — the 12-mile branch from Addison into Dallas came later, in 1903. headway_min is an ESTIMATE.
sources: NOT SOURCED AT SEGMENT LEVEL: the 1887 completion and 1888 arrival at Grapevine are carried by the references below, but no timetable was checked for this line's own trains, and the two dates conflict — see the layer's not_yet_sourced note.

segments.note: Under Southern Pacific control from 14 April 1932, and cut three years later: the Cotton Belt ended passenger service west of Addison in the summer of 1935, the last run being a westbound train to Fort Worth on 17 August 1935 — months before the railroad filed for bankruptcy that December, and 24 years before passenger service ended on the rest of the system. Freight continued, and TEXRail commuter trains run this alignment today, but neither is drawn here. headway_min is an ESTIMATE.
sources: Segment-level: the summer 1935 end of passenger service and the 17 August 1935 last westbound run to Fort Worth are stated by the Cotton Belt Depot Museum's Carrollton history.

properties.speed_source: ESTIMATE, not sourced. 40 km/h (25 mph) is a guess at a stopping local, and for the later years a mixed train, over a 200-mile line with many small-town stops.
properties.geometry_quality: Traced from OpenStreetMap: 199.7 mi over ways tagged old_railway_operator=SSW, live rail from Mount Pleasant through Pittsburg, Gilmer, Big Sandy, Tyler and Athens to Corsicana (UP's Pine Bluff and Corsicana Subdivisions), then railway=razed ways for the abandoned Corsicana – Dawson – Waco line. Three connectors totalling 2.2 km, the largest 1.6 km, all on the razed portion. The Waco end stops about 2 km short of the city centre where the mapped right of way ends. Per-leg mileages match the documented ones: Mount Pleasant – Tyler 67 mi, Tyler – Corsicana 74 mi, Corsicana – Waco 59 mi. Douglas-Peucker simplified at 15 m. Straight-line repair 2026-08-29: 1 ruled segment totalling 13 mi replaced with OpenStreetMap-traced rail geometry (see geometry_repairs for the OSM lines each one followed).

segments.note: This, not the Dallas line, was the Cotton Belt's Texas main line: TSHA describes the company's main track as running from Texarkana to Gatesville, with Mount Pleasant – Fort Worth as a branch off it. Its oldest piece is the Tyler Tap, opened Tyler – Big Sandy on 1 October 1877; Athens – Corsicana opened in 1881 and the 102 miles from Corsicana through Waco to Gatesville in 1882. Tyler was the company's Texas headquarters and shop town. Drawn from 1882, when the line was complete to Waco. headway_min is an ESTIMATE.
sources: NOT SOURCED AT SEGMENT LEVEL: the 1877, 1881 and 1882 construction dates are from the references below, but no timetable was checked for what passenger service ran on this line in this era.

segments.note: Under Southern Pacific control from 14 April 1932. The Cotton Belt ran passenger trains between Mount Pleasant, Tyler and Waco, plus a gas-electric doodlebug on the Tyler – Lufkin branch which is not drawn here. In 1949 the railroad still had 25 steam locomotives and four motor cars assigned to passenger work; by late 1952 nine diesels had replaced them and passenger mileage had been cut hard. headway_min is an ESTIMATE.
sources: NOT SOURCED AT SEGMENT LEVEL: Wikipedia names the Mount Pleasant – Tyler – Waco service and the 1949 and 1952 equipment counts, but gives no schedule or train numbers for this line.

segments.note: After the November 1952 restructuring the Memphis – Dallas Lone Star was replaced by trains 107 and 108, which connected with the Cotton Belt main line at Mount Pleasant. Service on this line ran out as mixed trains: the last one to Gatesville, beyond Waco, was discontinued in 1958. The end year drawn here is that 1958 date, applied to the whole Mount Pleasant – Waco line; see the layer's not_yet_sourced note. headway_min is an ESTIMATE.
sources: NOT SOURCED AT SEGMENT LEVEL: trains 107/108 and the Mount Pleasant connection come from the Lone Star article; the 1958 end of the Gatesville mixed train is from the publisher's description of Steve Goen's Passenger Trains of Texas: Cotton Belt. Neither states when Tyler – Waco itself lost its last passenger train.
